books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.text:
“...all freedmen, free negroes and mulattoes in this State, over the age of eighteen years, found on the second Monday in January, 1866, or thereafter, with no lawful employment or business, or found unlawfully assembling themselves together, either in the day or night time, and all white persons so assembling themselves with freedmen, free negroes or mulattoes, or usually associating with freedmen, free negroes or mulattoes, on terms of equality, or living in adultery or fornication with a freed woman, free negro or mulatto, shall be deemed vagrants. . . .”

—Mississippi Vagrant Law, part of the Mississippi Black Code, 1865
stimulus.source_note: Mississippi Vagrant Law (1865), Laws of Mississippi, 1865. Public domain. Wording verified against the transcription of the Laws of Mississippi text. Leading and trailing ellipses mark omitted text.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The Black Codes, including this law, most directly led Congress to

options.text: pass the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and propose the Fourteenth Amendment.
end the Freedmen’s Bureau at once and send its teachers home.
options.misconception: Background: Congress did the opposite, voting to extend the Bureau’s life over Johnson’s veto.

options.text: readmit the Southern states without conditions.
options.misconception: Background: the codes made Congress demand more conditions, not fewer.
Background: no one in Congress moved to repeal the Thirteenth Amendment, which had just been ratified.

rationales.A: Northerners read the codes as proof that Southern states would rebuild slavery by law if left alone. Congress answered with a civil rights law, then wrote citizenship and equal protection into the Constitution itself.
rationales.B: Background: Congress did the opposite, voting to extend the Bureau’s life over Johnson’s veto.
rationales.C: Background: the codes made Congress demand more conditions, not fewer.
rationales.D: Background: no one in Congress moved to repeal the Thirteenth Amendment, which had just been ratified.
rationales.general:
1. The codes showed Southern legislatures rebuilding slavery’s rules under new names.
2. Background: Northern voters had just fought a war to end slavery, and the codes looked like a lost peace.
3. Congress decided state promises were not enough and wrote rights into federal law and the Constitution.
4. The codes, meant to keep freedpeople down, pushed Congress further than it had planned to go.
Remember: a backlash can hand its opponents the argument they needed.
